implementation_notes: JavaScript closures are the original and most-used form: every function expression creates one, and it captures the enclosing lexical scope. The language's var/let distinction decides the failure mode - var is function-scoped and shared, so a handler created in a var loop sees the final value, while let is block-scoped and per-iteration, so the same loop is correct. Arrow functions inherit this lexically, which is why they are the correct choice for callbacks and class methods and function expressions are not. Memory: a handler registered on a long-lived target and capturing that target is the standard leak, and WeakRef plus FinalizationRegistry are the modern way to express the weak registration that addEventListener lacks.
idiom_name: function expression or arrow function capturing its lexical scope; per-iteration let binding
pitfalls: Capturing the loop variable in a var loop or in a reassigned outer variable produces late binding that only shows up at click time.
A handler on a long-lived target that captures a short-lived node keeps that node - and everything it references - alive until the handler is removed.
Arrow functions have no own 'this', so an arrow used as a class method or object method silently loses the receiver; use method shorthand for objects and prototypes for classes.
Binding a method with .bind(m) captures 'm' permanently; pass the receiver as an argument when the object outlives the binding.
